messages.subject: CC Variants
messages.body_plain:
Hey Karl,
When plotting the snp associations for one of our phenotypes, we noticed a large portion of Chr 14 with no snps.

I downloaded a fresh version of CC_variants.sqlite and when I directly query variants from the database I see that there are no snps for the region 25.87502-26.29484 Mbp. Is this normal? Is it just a region that has very little variation among the founders? Pulling up MGI SNP browser, I do see 1080 SNPs for the DO/CC founders within the 419,821 bp region although the coverage is pretty low in some areas.

This just looks odd in our figures and I haven't come across this before so I am trying to determine whether I have a problem or have a good explanation for it if not. Also, could this be what we are mapping to, some artifact?

Thanks,
Jessica

messages.subject: Re: CC Variants
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for pointing this out. I'm not sure the cause, but this gap does appear to be present in the Sanger SNP data.

The cc_variants.sqlite file is built from the sanger SNPs, indels, and structural variants VCF files.
The script that does the work is distributed with R/qtl2:
    https://github.com/rqtl/qtl2/blob/main/inst/scripts/create_ccvariants.R

The SNP files for build 38 are at https://ftp.ebi.ac.uk/pub/databases/mousegenomes/REL-1505-SNPs_Indels/
I was grabbing copies that are at JAX, in particular this one: ftp://ftp.jax.org/SNPtools/variants/mgp.v5.merged.snps_all.dbSNP142.vcf.gz

Poking through the copy of the file that I have, it does have that big gap that you identified. I'm not sure whether the problem is in my copy or in the original sanger file, or what the cause might be. I'm downloading fresh copies, but it's going to take a couple of hours.

We might look at the build 39 files to see if there are similar problems.

karl

messages.subject: GWAS analysis using R/qtl2?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Karl,
I have been told it is possible to do GWAS analyses using qtl2. I've been looking into the user guides ect., the best example I think I could use is 'DO' (diversity outbred) population. But still I am not sure, and don't know how to proceed with data formatting.
I have SNP matrix (with 0,1, 2), genetic map and my phenotype data ready. We have successfully used this dataset for GWAS with other package. however, the package we were using cannot incorporate weights in the scan.

Any guidance that would get me started would be greatly appreciated.

messages.subject: Re: GWAS analysis using R/qtl2?
messages.body_plain:
R/qtl2 is for analysis of experimental crosses from inbred lines. The DO population is a specific kind of advanced intercross population derived from eight inbred founder lines. The package is not really appropriate for generic GWAS, and requires genotype data on the founder lines.

What sort of population are you working with?

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl2-disc] Re: GWAS analysis using R/qtl2?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Karl,
We are working on a diversity panel of switchgrass.
We have about 600 genotypes grown at 10 locations across the US. Instead of doing GWAS for each location, we used a Finlay-Wilkinson (FW) (https://academic.oup.com/g3journal/article/6/3/589/6031117) approach to estimate the slope and intercept for each genotype and do the mapping for the intercept and slope.
Then we used the lab-developed SwtichgrassGWAS package (https://github.com/Alice-MacQueen/switchgrassGWAS) which is based on bigsnpr. This is fine, however, we want to take into account the error estimated from FW method into the mapping as weight.

We've used Rqtl2 for switchgrass 4-way population, and we were able to incorporate weights (or propagate the error) into the QTL mapping.
Now we are thinking about the similar stuff for the GWAS analyses. That's why I got all these questions. We don't have founder lines. We have snp data that was mapped onto a reference genome (AP13).

This is a partial email quote from my supervisor (Thomas E Juneger at UT Austin):
"Saunak says Rqtl2 has a GWAS function, and that data just needs to be formatted for it.  We should look at the rqtl2 google group –it might even make sense to ask Karl Broman a question that way…."
BTW, Dr. Saunak is a Professor and Chief of Biostatistics Professor in the University of Tennessee, he has been working  a lot on QTL mapping. Maybe he was mistaken.

messages.subject: Updated resources for mouse genome build GRCm39
messages.subject_clean: Updated resources for mouse genome build GRCm39
messages.body_plain:
The new mouse genome build GRCm39 has been out for almost 3 years.

For those involved in mouse genetics, particularly with CC/DO mice and the MUGA SNP arrays, I've created a page that points to the updated versions of our various resources
(revised genetic maps, array annotations, an R package for converting positions, files with founder SNP genotypes, and SQLite database of founder variant genotypes):

    https://kbroman.org/qtl2/pages/move_to_build39.html

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl2-disc] Re: CC Variants
messages.body_plain:
As Dan pointed out, the big changes in the “new” (as of June, 2020) mouse genome build GRCm39 are on chr 10 and 14, so if you have a QTL on those chromosomes, it would be particularly important to switch to the new build.

I think we finally have all of the necessary materials for QTL analysis with GRCm39, and this morning I wrote a document pointing to them <https://kbroman.org/qtl2/pages/move_to_build39.html>. The key things here:

- If you’re genotypes are from MegaMUGA/GigaMUGA, you can use the mmconvert package <https://github.com/rqtl/mmconvert> to convert your cross2 object to the new build

- There’s a new SQLite database for CC founders variants <https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.22630642.v1>, using the GRCm39 build. It includes ensembl gene information as well, but if you want to query the genes table, you have to use create_gene_query_func() with additional arguments, as the field names don’t match the defaults.

karl

messages.subject: R/qtl2 version 0.32
messages.body_plain:
A new version of R/qtl2 (version 0.32) has been released on CRAN. Windows and Mac binaries will be available within a few days.

The main changes include additional arguments in create_variant_query_func() and create_gene_query_func(), which allow additional flexibility but might break working code, and new function smooth_gmap() for smoothing out a genetic map, particularly to eliminate intervals with 0 recombination.

A complete list of changes is at https://github.com/rqtl/qtl2/blob/main/NEWS.md

Karl Broman

messages.subject: Genetic map
messages.body_plain:
I am trying to perform haplotype reconstruction with Low pass WGS data.

I have a list of RSID(s) that represents the genotypes in DO mice. I was able to create the Genotype data and the physical map. However, I am unable to run the probability computation without a genetic map.

I looked into the genetic markers (cM) available in the MGI, however mapping them to the RSIDs seems difficult.

I will appreciate any help in this regard.

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl2-disc] Genetic map
messages.body_plain:
I’d recommend using the markers’ physical positions to get estimated cM positions along a reference map, such as the Cox et al. genetic map. The mmconvert package can be used for this, for getting estimating genetic positions based on GRCm39 physical positions.

    https://github.com/rqtl/mmconvert

I’d be happy to provide further details if you need them.

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl2-disc] Genetic map
messages.body_plain:
I would recommend moving your marker positions to build 39 and then grabbing the corresponding cM positions.
And you may want to go back and re-analyze the low-pass WGS data using build 39.

If you have strong desire to stay with build 39, you can grab the older version of the Cox map from

   https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kbroman/CoxMapV3/main/OrigMaps/CoxMaps_rev_build38.csv

You can then use qtl2::interp_map to interpolate your positions.

karl
